units.title: Sorting contracts, lower bounds and merge sort
outcomes: State the sorting contract (stability, in-place behavior, comparator rules) and pick merge sort, quicksort or heap sort from the binding constraint.
Prove the comparison-sorting lower bound with a decision-tree argument and explain why counting and radix sorts escape it.
Implement stable top-down merge sort with a shared auxiliary buffer and check it against sorted with randomized differential tests.
units.why: Sorting is the first place an ordering invariant pays off, and the lower bound tells you when to stop tuning comparisons and change the input assumptions instead.

study.title: Linear-time sorts: counting, radix, bucket
study.locator: Three preconditions, three algorithms; Counting sort
study.depth: Skim LSD radix sort and Bucket sort for their preconditions only (fixed-width keys; near-uniform keys). Only counting sort is implemented here.

focus: Stability means equal keys keep their input order. Merge sort is stable because the merge emits the left run on ties (<=, not <). Quicksort and heap sort are not stable.

The merge recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) gives Theta(n log n) in the best, average and worst case. The shared buffer costs Theta(n) extra space plus Theta(log n) stack; the already-sorted short-circuit recovers Theta(n) on sorted input.

The lower bound counts leaves: n distinct keys admit n! permutations, so a decision tree needs height at least lg(n!), which is Omega(n log n) by Stirling. It binds only comparison sorts on general input; counting sort never compares and needs bounded integer keys instead.

Equal asymptotics do not mean equal speed in Python. On the author's machine (12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K, Python 3.13.14), a pure-Python merge sort on 20,000 random ints took 0.018 s against 0.0017 s for list.sort, about 10x. State the CPU and version with every timing you report.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement top-down merge sort with one shared auxiliary buffer, midpoint lo + (hi - lo)//2, <= in the merge, and the already-sorted short-circuit. On [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6] it must return [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Stability check: [(5, 'a'), (3, 'b'), (5, 'c')] must come back [(3, 'b'), (5, 'a'), (5, 'c')]. Then run a Hypothesis differential test against sorted on 300 lists up to length 60 with seed 0.
traps: Using < instead of <= in the merge. Ties taken from the right run break stability silently while every sortedness test still passes.
Allocating a fresh auxiliary list in every merge call. Allocate once at the top; per-call allocation adds a hidden linear factor at each of the log n levels.
Reading the lower bound as a ban on fast sorting. It bans fast comparison sorting on general input; bounded keys (counting) or fixed-width keys (radix) change the model and the bound does not apply.

selfTest.q: Prove that any comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
selfTest.a: Model the sort as a decision tree: each internal node is one comparison and each leaf is one output permutation. Sorting n distinct keys needs at least n! leaves. A binary tree with L leaves has height at least lg L, so the height is at least lg(n!). By Stirling, n! > (n/e)^n, so lg(n!) > n lg n - n lg e = Omega(n log n).

selfTest.q: Why does counting sort not contradict that bound?
selfTest.a: The bound counts comparisons on general input. Counting sort never compares keys; it indexes by key value, which needs bounded integer keys with k = O(n) for linear time. Change the assumption and the bound does not apply.

selfTest.q: Is Python's list.sort stable, and how do you check from a REPL?
selfTest.a: Yes, it is Timsort and stable. Check sorted([(5, 'a'), (3, 'b'), (5, 'c')], key=lambda p: p[0]): the two 5s keep the order ('a') before ('c').

selfTest.q: Why does merge sort cost Theta(n log n) even on already-sorted input without the short-circuit?
selfTest.a: Every level still visits all n elements to merge, and there are about log2 n levels regardless of order. The short-circuit only skips the merge work when the two runs are already ordered, which recovers Theta(n) on sorted input.

study.title: Quickselect vs heap for top-K
study.locator: The decision; Algorithms compared; Side-by-side; Common misconceptions

focus: Lomuto invariant: at every scan step, arr[lo..i] holds elements <= pivot, arr[i+1..j-1] holds elements > pivot, and arr[j..hi-1] is unexamined. The final swap puts the pivot at its final sorted index. Median-of-three places the pivot at arr[hi]; that placement is part of the contract.

Strict < in the partition sends equal keys right. On all-equal input Lomuto still degenerates to Theta(n^2) even with a random pivot; three-way (Dutch flag) partition groups equal keys in one pass and recovers Theta(n).
Random pivot is the correctness fix, not an optimization: naive last-element pivot is Theta(n^2) on sorted input, and LC 215 hides a 50,000-element sorted test that times a fixed pivot out.

Top-k routing: a stream or tiny k favors a size-k heap (O(n log k) time, O(k) space, no mutation); a whole array in memory with unsorted output favors quickselect (expected O(n)); sorted output adds O(k log k). In CPython, heapq.nlargest runs in C: on the author's machine (12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K, Python 3.13.14) it took 0.001 s against 0.014 s for pure-Python quickselect on 100,000 ints with k=100, so count comparisons and wall-clock separately.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement Lomuto partition with a random pivot swap and iterative quickselect for kth largest. Assert the post-condition on every partition call (pivot at its final index, left band strictly less, right band greater or equal). With random.seed(215), quickselect([3,2,1,5,6,4], 2) must return 5. Run a Hypothesis differential test against sorted on 300 lists up to length 40, including sorted and all-equal inputs.
traps: Converting k wrong: kth largest wants target index n-k, kth smallest wants k-1. For n=6, k=2, the target index is 4.
Quickselect mutates the caller's array. Copy at the boundary when the caller needs the input intact.
Recursing into the wrong side after partition. The pivot sits at its final sorted position; only the side containing the target index is read again. The rest is partitioned, not sorted.

selfTest.q: State the Lomuto invariant and what the final swap establishes.
selfTest.a: During the scan, arr[lo..i] holds elements <= pivot, arr[i+1..j-1] holds elements > pivot, and arr[j..hi-1] is unexamined. The final swap moves the pivot just past the <= band, so it sits at its final sorted index with everything left <= it and everything right > it.

selfTest.q: Why does Lomuto with a random pivot still go quadratic on all-equal input, and what fixes it?
selfTest.a: Strict < sends every equal key to the right band, so each partition peels off one element and T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n) = Theta(n^2). Three-way partition groups all pivot-equal keys in one pass, so the recursion skips them and the cost is Theta(n).

selfTest.q: When does a size-k heap beat quickselect for top-k, and when does it lose asymptotically?
selfTest.a: The heap wins when the input streams (quickselect needs random access to the whole array) or when O(k) space without mutation matters. At k = n/2 the heap costs O(n log n) and loses its edge while quickselect stays expected O(n). Sorted output adds O(k log k) on top of either.

selfTest.q: What does introselect change about quickselect's worst case?
selfTest.a: It watches the recursion depth and falls back to a worst-case-linear method past about 2 lg n depth, which caps the adversarial case. The fallback proof belongs to algorithms/decomposition-greedy-randomness/divide-conquer-recurrences.

units.title: Binary search: intervals, bounds and feasibility predicates
outcomes: Prove the binary-search loop invariant and derive safe boundary updates for lower-bound, upper-bound and first-true variants.
Implement exact-match, lower-bound, upper-bound and answer-space search from the invariant, with differential tests against bisect.
Turn a monotone feasibility predicate into lo/hi bounds with cost O(F log W), and defend why monotonicity (not sortedness) is the requirement.
units.why: Binary search fails in production through boundary bugs, not through asymptotics. One invariant derives every variant, and the same invariant searches answer spaces that are not arrays at all.

study.title: Algorithmica: Binary Search
study.depth: Read for the branch-prediction and cache explanation only. Every speedup number there (2.5x to 3x branchless on small arrays, about 2x Eytzinger against std::lower_bound) is a C++ measurement with Clang 10 on Zen 2; do not transfer any crossover point to Python.

focus: Closed [lo,hi] pairs with while lo <= hi and hi=mid-1; half-open [lo,hi) pairs with while lo < hi and hi=mid. Mixing the pairs is the non-termination bug.
lower_bound keeps equality right with nums[mid] < target; upper_bound keeps equality left with nums[mid] <= target. Their difference counts duplicates.
Answer-space search is Template C with a monotone predicate: feasibility must hold above (or below) a threshold with no gaps. Cost is O(F log W) for predicate cost F and width W.

Algorithmica's C++ numbers explain why equal-asymptotic searches cross over (an unpredictable branch costs 10 to 15 cycles, a cache miss up to 300), but Python's interpreter overhead moves every crossover. Verify bounds against bisect, not against ported constants.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement lower_bound, upper_bound and a first-true search on [lo,hi). On [1,2,2,2,3] with target 2, return 1 and 4. Reproduce Koko: piles [3,6,7,11] with h=8 must return 4. Run a Hypothesis differential test of both bounds against bisect_left and bisect_right on 300 sorted lists up to length 30.
traps: Returning lo for every template. The upper-bound twin and Template A need their own return values; derive each from the invariant instead of memorizing one.
Writing lo=mid or hi=mid in Template A after a miss. The closed interval needs mid+1 and mid-1 to shrink; the half-open forms are the ones that keep mid.
Searching on a predicate that is not monotone. Prove hours(k) is nonincreasing in k (or your predicate's direction) before trusting the loop; a gap in feasibility silently returns a wrong answer.

selfTest.q: Prove Template B terminates with lo at the lower bound.
selfTest.a: Invariant: every index j < lo has nums[j] < target and every index k >= hi has nums[k] >= target. Each iteration replaces [lo,hi) with a strictly smaller half that preserves the invariant, since mid sits strictly inside while lo < hi. The width shrinks to zero, so lo == hi; the invariant then says every index below lo is < target while nums[lo] >= target, so lo is the lower bound.

selfTest.q: On [1,2,2,2,3], what do exact-match search, lower_bound and upper_bound return for target 2, and why?
selfTest.a: Exact match returns some index in {1,2,3}. lower_bound returns 1 because the strict comparison keeps equality right; upper_bound returns 4 because the non-strict comparison keeps equality left. The duplicate count is 4 - 1 = 3.

selfTest.q: Why is binary search correct on the Koko predicate when speeds are not stored in an array?
selfTest.a: hours(k) is nonincreasing in k: a faster speed never needs more hours. That monotonicity is the only requirement; the loop searches the predicate, not a sorted array. Each probe scans n piles, so the cost is O(n log max(piles)).

selfTest.q: A colleague ports Algorithmica's branchless binary search to Python expecting 2.5x. What do you tell them?
selfTest.a: The 2.5x to 3x number is Algorithmica's C++ measurement (Clang 10, Zen 2) on small arrays. Python's per-iteration interpreter overhead dominates and removes the branch-prediction effect, so the constant does not transfer. Measure with timeit on the real workload instead.
